newsitem.title: GERMANY: FOCUS-Bonn mulling Telekom stake sale.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-Bonn mulling Telekom stake sale.

text.p: German Finance Minister Theo Waigel mooted plans on Wednesday for selling another stake in Deutsche Telekom AG ahead of schedule in an apparent bid to cut Bonn's borrowing needs before the single European single currency is launched.
With Bonn struggling to meet the entry criteria for economic and monetary union (EMU), Waigel said an early sale of Telekom shares still held by the government was possible.
"It is conceivable that parts of the privatisation of Telekom could be brought forward," he told reporters.

Telekom launched Europe's largest share listing last November, putting around 25 percent of the company's capital in public hands in a $13 billion initial public offering (IPO). The state still holds the rest.
Waigel said he did not expect an early sale would hit Telekom or the around two million private shareholders who took part in the company's landmark float.
"With the company's exquisite state of health a sale of shares would not be a problem," Waigel said.
"We have more than 70 percent in Telekom and we don't need that much. A company and its share price that have blossomed and flourished like Telekom does not need the government," he added.
German law does not explicitly rule out the government selling its shares before the year 2000, but it had been widely believed that this would be possible only under extraordinary circumstances.

Telekom chairman Ron Sommer told Bild newspaper that German law required the government to seek approval from the Telekom management board for a sale of shares that would affect the market before December 31, 1999.

"Such a measure requires the approval of the management board," he was quoted as saying in a report to appear on Thursday. "We will ensure that the interests of the nearly two million shareholders are not affected. There is complete agreement on this point between the finance minister and myself."

A finance ministry spokeswoman stressed that should the government sell its shares, it would avoid doing so in a way that could damage Telekom's financial situation or the interests of existing shareholders.

Germany changed the constitution and drafted its Telecommunications Act to allow the Telekom privatisation, stating the government would not under normal circumstances be allowed to sell its remaining shares until the year 2000.
But the telecoms law does not explicitly rule out an early sale of the government's stake.
The news put pressure on Telekom shares, which fell 93 pfennigs to 39.20 marks in the afternoon.

Some dealers were uncertain whether the government would actually put the shares into the market. The German post ministry said the law made clear that the shares could not be sold in the open market before the year 2000.
An alternative would be for Bonn to transfer its Telekom holdings to the Kreditanstalt fuer Wiederaufbau, as it did with its remaining Lufthansa shares last year.
In any event, it appears that the government will do all it can to avoid scaring off nearly two million private investors who took part in the IPO last November by moving shares to the market gently.
Waigel repeated this, calling the company's landmark listing last November a success and noting that its competitive position was strong.
"I think it would be right that we continue the privatisation in appropriate tranches that are bearable by the stock market," he said.
